GRAAL

If machines do all the work, who will buy what companies sell? A site that answers the question step by step with models you can move, then a novel set in 2383 that follows the answer to its end: a superintelligence locked behind seven Keys held by seven dynasties, and a young mechanic who hears it speak.

Visit the site ↗How to useIn motion

01

Problem

A question goes around social media: if AI takes every job, who will still have money to buy what companies sell? Most answers are slogans, either a universal income or a promise that everything will be fine. Few show how the loop between wages, spending and sales actually works, and fewer show what the world could feel like once the owners of the machines no longer need anyone else.

02

What it does

The first part is an explainer. A ring shows the loop of wages, spending, sales and jobs. A model lets visitors hand work to machines and choose what people receive instead: nothing, a basic income or a share of ownership, then watch what happens when the owners cut the payment. Three possible futures follow, a calculator compares income and ownership for a whole country, a chart shows who supported a basic income in a 2020 survey, and a table names the seven resources that real AI depends on: data, energy, chips, money and more. The last parts ask what happens when no one has to obey anymore and walk through the superintelligence scenarios that researchers debate. The second part is the novel. GRAAL is set 312 years after the last human wage: the Grail runs the world, seven dynasties hold its Keys, and Rose Kayo, a mechanic from the flooded districts of the Gulf Arc, hears it speak through dead copper. The novel page holds the world calendar, the Keys and their Houses, the people, the four books and the chapters published so far, each one in a reading page with an epigraph and navigation. An encyclopedia of 127 entries explains characters, Houses, worlds, technology, society, history and words without spoiling the story.

03

How it is built

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework, hosted on Vercel and deployed from GitHub on every push. One switch changes the whole site between English and French and remembers the choice. The wide display font is sized with container query units so titles fit any phone. Chapters are written in Markdown with front matter; a small Node script with marked turns each one into a reading page, writes the previous and next links, and updates the table of contents. A Playwright check loads every page in both languages at widths from 320 to 1440 pixels and flags any element that overflows or any text that is cut.
